deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivations. It is a short programmatic self-description by Riemann: a statement of his current research, signed 'B. Riemann.' It was published posthumously by Weber and Dedekind as the opening of the 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts' (Naturphilosophie) in Riemann's Gesammelte mathematische Werke (1876). Its content, point by point:

(1) Riemann proposes to do for other transcendental functions what had already been done for algebraic functions, the exponential and circular functions, and the elliptic and Abelian functions: to introduce 'das Imaginäre', that is, to study them as functions of a complex variable. He says the necessary general groundwork is in his Inaugural Dissertation (1851), Art. 20. That article explains how the dissertation's principles (determining a function by its boundary values and discontinuities on a Riemann surface) should give access to transcendental functions. The programme was realised, for example, in the 1857 treatment of the Gauss hypergeometric series via the P-function and monodromy, and in the posthumous work on linear differential equations with algebraic coefficients.

(2) Connected with this are new methods for integrating partial differential equations, which he says he has already applied with success to several physical problems. Plausible referents are the 1854/55 Nobili-rings electrostatics, heat conduction, and later the 1860 method for linear hyperbolic equations: the Riemann function for sound waves of finite amplitude.

(3) His 'Hauptarbeit' is a new conception of the known laws of nature, expressed through other fundamental concepts. This is meant to make the experimental data on the interactions of heat, light, magnetism and electricity usable for discovering how they are connected (a unified ether/field programme). He names Newton, Euler and Herbart as his chief influences. He accepts almost completely Herbart's earliest results, the doctoral and habilitation theses of 22 and 23 October 1802. He departs from Herbart's later speculation on one essential point, and this produces differences regarding Herbart's Naturphilosophie and the parts of psychology connected to it.

The pencil margin note is a reference, likely editorial, to Herbart's Sämmtliche Werke, ed. Hartenstein, Bd. 12, S. 58–59, where those theses are printed. There is no mathematics to reconstruct.

results.what: New methods for integrating PDEs applied to physical problems
results.modern_name: Riemann's methods in mathematical physics (e.g. Riemann's method / Riemann function for hyperbolic equations, 1860)

results.modern_name: Riemann's Naturphilosophie / ether-field programme (precursor of field-theoretic unification)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Riemann's well-known statement of research interests. It was published by Weber and Dedekind in the Gesammelte Werke and is frequently quoted in literature on Riemann and Herbart. The page has no new mathematical content.
transcription_corrections: Signature reads 'B. Riemann' (written as 'BRiemann'); the transcription is fine.

Margin note is most plausibly '[Sämmtl. Werke, hrsg. von Hartenstein, Bd. 12, S. 58, 59.]'. This is Herbart's collected works, giving the location of the 1802 theses, and is likely an editorial annotation rather than Riemann's text.
'über die Wechselwirkungen': a word after 'über' appears struck through and rewritten. The intended reading is 'über die Wechselwirkungen'.
Struck word before 'Verschiedenheit' is 'wesentl[iche]', correctly marked as deleted.
